summary: Internal SE/AE sparring session to practice contrarian objections and tighten demo messaging around latency/cost tradeoffs and private deployments. Focus on short demo scenes, phrasing for enterprise buyers (security, VPC, SOC2), and a checklist for fast-swappable model variants.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-05
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 64 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Blake (AE), Maya Lin (SE), Diego Ramos (SE), Samir Patel (Sales), Lena Ortiz (Sales), Evan Kline (PMM)
Drive links mentioned: https://drive.redwood/example/playbook-v1 (reference), benchmark sheet: https://drive.redwood/example/benchmarks

Summary (auto): 30-60 minute sparring followed by 20 min Q&A and action item capture. Practice quick rebuttals to cost/latency objections and two demo skits (1. hosted latency demo, 2. private deployment handoff).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: okay, um hi everyone thanks for squeezing this in today. this is, uh, the contrarian scrimmage, the goal is twofold, tighten up the 90-second demo scenes and practice the pushback when buyers say "we'll host it ourselves" or "cost is too high". Maya, you good to run scene one?
[00:18] Maya: yeah totally. I'll do the hosted-latency scene. Diego, you can jump in as the skeptic.
[00:22] Diego: cool, i'm on. just for context, i'm gonna be the infra lead that keeps bringing up KV cash issues and, uh, KMS.
[00:30] Samir: (quiet) I'll listen and scribble notes.
[00:34] Maya: ok scene one: quick pitch, "redwood inference gives you predictable latency for chat workloads with automatic batching and prefix KV cache."
[00:42] Diego: (interrupt) sorry, what was that? prefix K V cash? 
[00:45] Maya: yeah, prefix K V cache, sorry. I said KV cache, sometimes the transcription messes it up.
[00:51] Jordan: that's actually a good point to call out — the wording matters, people hear "cache" as unreliable. try: "we maintain a secure KV cache that preserves context across sessions and can be pinned per customer."
[01:03] Lena: can we call out the on-prem variant quickly? some enterprise buyers won't hear 'hosted' without thinking data residency.
[01:08] Maya: sure: "we offer hosted API for fast time-to-value, dedicated pools for committed throughput, and a private deployment option that runs in your VPC or on-prem with K M S integrations."
[01:20] Evan: careful — say 'K M S' too fast and it sounds like 'KMS' or 'CMS', maybe just say 'customer KMS/HSM'.
[01:26] Diego: and if they push us on cost, I want a short script: "we've got tooling—Redwood Optimize—that recommends batching and quantization profiles tied to your workload. it's not just a black box cost, it's tunable."
[01:40] Jordan: yep, and follow with an example: "in one io company we reduced unit costs by 35% using a combination of KV caching and quantized local variants" — placeholder anonymized case.
[01:51] Samir: question — don't we risk overpromising on quantization affect on quality? buyers push on 'how will answers change'.
[01:58] Maya: good point, say: "we measure quality continuously and provide regression alerts tied to your prompt sets; we can run before/after evals as part of the pilot."
[02:10] Diego: ok scene two, private deploy handoff. Jordan you start as the CISO, I'll be the SE walking through audit controls.
[02:17] Jordan: fine, here's my contrarian line: "we can't run third-party software in our VPC — it's a hard no unless there's a full air gap or HSM-backed keys."
[02:26] Diego: response: "we offer an on-prem package and a private control plane option; you can manage your network and keys, we integrate to your KMS or HSM and provide audit logs and SOC 2 artifacts. we can also do an in-person runbook review for your audit team."
[02:42] Jordan: pushback — buyer asks about performance for a 2s SLO on short prompts and our cost per 1k tokens vs other vendors.
[02:50] Maya: quick reply: "we provide model profiles and verified performance for common sequence lengths; we can pin model variants and do a canary rollout so you get predictable latency while we tune batching windows. and we'll give you the cost knobs so you can balance latency and unit economics."
[03:06] Lena: practical note — add a one-line cost-compare script: "for X prompt mix, hosted with caching was Y cents/token, dedicated reserved was Z cents/token at commit" — have numbers ready in the sheet.
[03:18] Jordan: Diego, you had a disruptive competitor play, right? how do we handle "we already use Anthropic/OpenAI for gen"?
[03:24] Diego: yeah typical — lead with differentiation not feature dumping: "many teams start there for convenience; Redwood's edge is production economics and operational controls — if you're optimizing for predictable latency and isolation, this is where we add value. we can also run an apples-to-apples benchmark during the pilot."
[03:40] Samir: do we have a one-liner to beat the 'ease of use' argument? like when they say 'we'll just go with the big public API'?
[03:46] Maya: something like: "public APIs are quick to start but they bury unit economics and have limited options for private deployments and enterprise SLAs — Redwood is the next step for teams moving from prototype to mission-critical."
[03:58] Evan: add a line on observability: "we expose per-route token breakdowns, traces, and rollout audits so you can measure the cost impact of every change."
[04:07] Jordan: great. now lightning roleplay — each of you get 30s to handle the 'too expensive' objection. Diego first.
[04:12] Diego: (1) empathize, (2) quantify: "i hear that, cost is real. quick scan — with simple batching and a cache policy we usually see 20-40% savings; if you give us a prompt sample we'll run a token-cost projection and show the tradeoffs."
[04:26] Maya: (short) "we don't ask you to choose blind; our Optimize tool makes suggestions and we can run a short POC with explicit metrics so you can see the delta before commit."
[04:36] Samir: Jordan, you're the buyer — what else do you want to hear to get comfortable?
[04:40] Jordan: track record and security. show me a SOC2 or an equivalent pack, show me role-based access, and show me how keys are handled so my legal team relaxes.
[04:49] Lena: make a call-out in the deck to the security appendix and to the private deployment checklist. not everyone reads the appendices so say it aloud in the demo.
[04:58] Evan: also call out the rollout patterns — canary, A/B, automatic fallback to cheaper variant — the resilience angle sells well.
[05:06] Maya: short demo idea — "simulate a canary rollback" in the console view: we flip traffic, show latency graph updating and then fallback. keeps it tangible.
[05:15] Jordan: ok we spent the first 20 min on skits. let's move to two-minute rapid-fire rebuttal phrases and then Q&A.
[05:23] Diego: phrase bank example: "we can constrain variance with pinned model versions and automated rollouts so you don't get sudden regressions" — short and concrete.
[05:33] Samir: a lot of reps asked about 'latency SLOs' — how to answer if they ask 'can you guarantee 100ms?'.
[05:39] Maya: don't guarantee unrealistic numbers; say "we have tuned profiles and verified medians for common sequence lengths; we work with you to define SLOs and set an SLA on the dedicated offering."
[05:49] Jordan: note for the playbook — include a table: sequence length -> expected median/95th p99 for hosted/dedicated. Diego, can you draft that?
[05:57] Diego: yes, I'll sketch a CSV and drop in the benchmark sheet.
[06:01] (longer section: tradecraft tips)
[06:05] Maya: tip — use a 90s 'start to finish' demo that always ends with a win: e.g., show a live chat, then show rollback, then show cost delta in the console. keep it repeatable.
[06:16] Samir: we should have a two-slide appendix with pre-baked numbers and strings for each objection.
[06:21] Lena: and a short 'security script' for legal: "we offer an on-prem package, audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration, and SOC 2 evidence" — practice saying that in 20 seconds.
[06:34] Jordan: okay, final section — we'd like to capture any unusual objections you saw in the field. Samir, quick list.
[06:39] Samir: (rapid) "we can't afford vendor lock-in"; "we need full offline inference"; "we have to use our in-house models only"; "pricing is opaque".
[06:48] Maya: responses: lock-in — "we support standard model formats and a consistent API so migration is straightforward; we also provide canary/export tools." offline inference — "we have an on-prem package and salted air-gap option for regulated workloads".
[06:59] Diego: in-house models — "we can serve customer-owned models in private deployments or work with you to optimize an open checkpoint for serving."
[07:09] Evan: pricing opaque — "we provide a per-token breakdown and a cost-analytics report during pilots so you can see exactly where spend goes."
[07:17] (Q&A)
[07:20] Lena: question — how deep do we go on quantization in a first call versus a later technical deep dive?
[07:25] Maya: first call: high level only, emphasize quality monitoring and pilot evals. deep dive: bring in runtime folks and show kernel/quantization tradeoff slides.
[07:35] Jordan: ok closing recap — we'll update the playbook, add the 90s demo scripts, populate the appendix with security phrases, and run the benchmark on the sample prompt set.
[07:45] Diego: I'll own the benchmarks, Jordan you'll own the playbook edits, Maya you'll craft the demo script.
[07:52] Jordan: perfect, thanks everyone. we'll reconvene briefly next week if v2 deck is ready.
[07:58] (meeting ends, small side chatter)

Notes: imperfect transcription observed for acronyms (KMS, SAML) and technical terms (KV cache sometimes as 'K V cash'), occasional speaker mislabels. The team referenced a shared drive with sample prompts and a benchmarking sheet; participants agreed to drop artifacts there.
